intro: A call to prayer rises from a mosque in Bridgeview. A family in Rogers Park breaks the Ramadan fast with a date and a glass of water. A student in Indonesia recites the same Arabic verses as a student in Chicago. About two billion people today call themselves Muslims, and Islam is one of the largest religions in the world.

This unit studies Islam the way a historian does. First you will follow Muhammad's life as Muslims tell it, learn how the Qur'an is organized and recited, and see the Five Pillars in daily life. Then you will trace how Muslim states, scholars and traders linked Spain, West Africa, Baghdad, India and Indonesia, and how Muslims came to America.

By the end, you will be able to explain key Muslim beliefs and practices in their own terms, describe the Sunni and Shia branches, place major events on a timeline, and use real sources, from the Qur'an to a traveler's diary, to support what you say.

title: Islam in History

chapters.title: Muhammad, the Qur'an and the First Community
chapters.bigQuestion: How did one man's message in a mountain cave become the faith of a whole community?

story.title: The Trustworthy One on the Mountain
story.kicker: A respected merchant of Mecca goes to a quiet cave to think, and Muslims say his life changed there.
paragraphs: Mecca, around the year 610. The city sits in a dry valley in western Arabia. Camel caravans come and go, carrying spices, cloth and leather. Traders from many tribes crowd its markets. At the center of the city stands the Kaaba, a cube-shaped building that Arabs from far away visit.

Among the merchants is a man of about forty named Muhammad. He lost his parents as a child and was raised by his grandfather and then his uncle. He works in the caravan trade. People in Mecca call him al-Amin, which means "the trustworthy." They leave their valuables with him because they know he is honest.

Muhammad often climbs a rocky mountain outside the city. Near the top is a small cave called Hira. There he spends nights alone, thinking and praying. According to Muslim tradition, one night in the month of Ramadan, the angel Gabriel (Jibril in Arabic) came to him in the cave.

Muslims tell that the angel gave one command: "Recite!" Muhammad answered that he was not a reciter. The command came again, and then the first words of what Muslims call the Qur'an. Shaken, Muhammad hurried home to his wife, Khadijah. She comforted him and, in Muslim tradition, became the first person to accept his message.

Over the next twenty-some years, Muslims believe, more revelations came. They were memorized, recited and later gathered into one book. Today about two billion people call themselves Muslims. This chapter follows the story as Muslims tell it and as historians study it.
story.think: Why do you think people in Mecca trusted Muhammad before he ever began to preach? Why might that matter to the story Muslims tell?

lessons.title: Arabia Before Islam
lessons.mainIdea: Before Islam, Arabia was a land of trading towns and desert tribes, with Mecca and its Kaaba at the center of trade and worship.
reading: Picture the Arabian Peninsula around 600 CE. Most of it is desert. People live in oasis towns or move with herds of camels and goats. They belong to *tribes*, large family groups that protect their members. Loyalty to the tribe mattered more than loyalty to any king, because Arabia had no single ruler.

Mecca was a trading town. Caravans carried goods between Yemen in the south and Syria in the north. The powerful Quraysh tribe ran much of this trade. Mecca also held the *Kaaba*, a stone shrine. Each year, people from many tribes came to worship there, and fighting was forbidden during certain months so pilgrims and traders could travel safely.

Most Arabs at this time worshipped many gods. In Muslim tradition, the Kaaba held hundreds of idols, or statues of gods. Some Arabs were Jews or Christians, and a few, called hanifs in Muslim sources, worshipped one God. Muslims call this time the Jahiliyya, meaning "the age of ignorance," because in their view it came before God's final message.

words.d: a large group of families who share an ancestor and protect one another
a cube-shaped shrine in Mecca; Muslims believe Abraham and his son Ishmael built it to worship one God
the leading tribe of Mecca, which Muhammad was born into

look.title: A Market Town and a Shrine
look.text: Mecca had little water and poor soil for farming. Yet it grew rich. Caravans stopped there on the road between Yemen and Syria. Pilgrims came to the Kaaba each year, and during the sacred months, tribes agreed not to fight.
look.prompt: How could a shrine and a trade route help each other? Give one way the pilgrims helped the merchants.

check.q: What was the Kaaba in Mecca before Islam?
choices: A shrine that people from many tribes visited
A royal palace for the king of Arabia
A school for studying the Qur'an
A Christian church built by the Romans
check.why: The Kaaba was a shrine at the center of Mecca, visited by people from many tribes.

check.q: Why did tribes matter so much in Arabia around 600 CE?
choices: The Roman emperor chose tribal leaders

Tribes were religious groups that each had one holy book
check.why: Arabia had no king over everyone, so a person's tribe gave protection.

check.q: What does the Arabic term Jahiliyya mean, as Muslims use it?
choices: The age of ignorance before Islam
check.why: Muslims use Jahiliyya, "the age of ignorance," for the time before the Qur'an's message.

lessons.title: The Cave and the Message
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims believe that around 610 CE, the angel Gabriel brought Muhammad the first words of the Qur'an in the cave of Hira.
reading: Muhammad was born in Mecca around 570 CE. He grew up as an orphan and became a trader. At about age twenty-five he married Khadijah, a widow who ran her own caravan business. As an adult, he often went to the cave of Hira to be alone and reflect.

Muslims believe that around 610 CE, the angel Gabriel came to him there with a message from God. They call these messages *revelation*, words that God makes known. The first words, in Muslim tradition, are the opening of Surah 96: a command to recite in the name of the Lord who created.

For Muslims, this night made Muhammad a *prophet*, a person God chooses to carry a message. The Qur'an describes him as the "seal of the prophets," the last in a line that Muslims say includes Abraham, Moses and Jesus. Jews and Christians have their own teachings about those figures and do not share this view of Muhammad.

words.d: a message that believers say God makes known to people
a person who, believers say, is chosen by God to deliver God's message
the mountain cave near Mecca where Muslims say the first revelation came

look.title: The First Words
look.text: Recite in the name of your Lord, who created. He created the human being from a clinging clot. Recite, for your Lord is most generous, who taught by the pen, taught people what they did not know.
look.cite: Qur'an, Surah 96 (al-Alaq), verses 1–5; paraphrased in plain English
look.prompt: The first words Muslims say were revealed are about reciting and the pen. What do they suggest about how Muslims value learning?

check.q: About when do Muslims date the first revelation to Muhammad?
check.why: Muslim tradition places the first revelation around 610 CE, when Muhammad was about forty.

check.q: Who was Khadijah?
choices: Muhammad's wife, who in Muslim tradition first accepted his message
The angel who brought the revelation
A queen of Yemen who attacked Mecca
check.why: Khadijah was Muhammad's wife; Muslims honor her as the first believer.

check.q: What does the Qur'an mean by calling Muhammad the "seal of the prophets"?
choices: Muslims believe he is the last prophet
He was the first prophet ever
check.why: Muslims read "seal of the prophets" to mean Muhammad is the final prophet.

lessons.title: From Mecca to Medina
lessons.mainIdea: In 622 Muhammad and his followers moved from Mecca to Medina, a journey called the hijra that starts the Islamic calendar.
reading: Muhammad began to preach in Mecca. He taught that there is one God, that people will be judged for their deeds, and that the rich must care for the poor. Some people joined him. Many leaders of the Quraysh did not. His message challenged the gods of the Kaaba and the trade that pilgrims brought.

The early Muslims faced insults, boycotts and violence. In 622, people from the town of Yathrib invited Muhammad to lead them. He and his followers moved there. This move is called the *hijra*, Arabic for "migration." Yathrib became known as Medina, "the city" of the Prophet.

In Medina, Muslims formed their first *umma*, or community. Muhammad was both its religious teacher and its leader. Medina also had Jewish tribes, and an agreement often called the Constitution of Medina set out rules for the town's groups. Muslims later made 622 the first year of their calendar.

words.d: the migration of Muhammad and his followers from Mecca to Medina in 622
the community of all Muslims
the city north of Mecca, once called Yathrib, where Muhammad led the first Muslim community

look.title: Why Start a Calendar Here?
look.text: Muslims could have started their calendar with Muhammad's birth or with the first revelation. Instead they chose the hijra in 622. That was the year the believers first lived together as a community with their own leader and rules.
look.prompt: Why might a community choose its move to Medina, not a birthday, as year one? What does the choice show about what Muslims value?

check.q: What was the hijra?
choices: The move from Mecca to Medina in 622
check.why: The hijra is the migration to Medina in 622.

check.q: Why did many Quraysh leaders oppose Muhammad's preaching?
choices: He asked them to move to Egypt
His message of one God challenged the gods of the Kaaba and the trade around it
He wanted to become king of Rome
He banned all trade in Mecca
check.why: Teaching one God questioned the Kaaba's idols, which drew pilgrims and trade.

check.q: Which event marks year one of the Islamic calendar?
check.why: The Islamic calendar counts its years from the hijra of 622.

lessons.title: Return to Mecca
lessons.mainIdea: In 630 Muhammad returned to Mecca, and Muslims rededicated the Kaaba to one God; he died in Medina in 632.
reading: For several years, Medina and Mecca were at war. Battles such as Badr (624) and Uhud (625) are well known in Muslim history. In 628 the two sides signed a truce at a place called Hudaybiyya. When the truce broke down, Muhammad marched toward Mecca with a large army in 630.

Mecca surrendered with little fighting. Muslim sources say Muhammad forgave most of his old enemies. He had the idols removed from the Kaaba. Muslims believe this returned the shrine to the worship of one God, as they say Abraham first intended. Many Arab tribes then joined the Muslim community.

In 632 Muhammad made a pilgrimage to Mecca and gave what Muslims call the *Farewell Sermon*. He died later that year in Medina. His followers faced a hard question: who should lead the community now? Their answers to that question still shape Islam today.

words.d: an agreement to stop fighting for a time
the speech Muslims say Muhammad gave at his last pilgrimage in 632

look.title: Key Years in Muhammad's Life
look.cite: Common dates from Muslim tradition and historians; early dates are approximate
look.prompt: How many years passed between the first revelation and Muhammad's death? How many of those years did he spend in Medina?

check.q: What did Muhammad do at the Kaaba after returning to Mecca in 630?
choices: He gave it to the Byzantine emperor
check.why: Muslim sources say he removed the idols and dedicated the Kaaba to one God.

check.q: In what year did Muhammad die?
check.why: Muhammad died in Medina in 632, after his final pilgrimage.

check.q: What big question did Muslims face after Muhammad's death?
choices: Whether to keep fasting in Ramadan
Whether to move back to Yathrib
check.why: Muhammad's death raised the question of leadership, which later divided Sunni and Shia.

lessons.title: A Book Meant to Be Recited
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims believe the Qur'an is God's word in Arabic, first memorized and recited, then gathered into one written book.
reading: The word *Qur'an* means "recitation." Muslims believe it is the exact word of God, given to Muhammad through Gabriel over about 23 years. At first, followers memorized the verses and wrote some on bone, leather and palm leaves. Reciting aloud was the main way people learned it.

Muslim tradition says the verses were collected into one book soon after Muhammad died. Under the third caliph, Uthman (ruled 644–656), a standard copy was made and sent to major cities. Muslims hold that the text has been kept the same since then.

Muslims believe the Qur'an is fully the Qur'an only in Arabic. Translations help readers understand the meaning, but most Muslims treat them as explanations, not as the Qur'an itself. Many Muslims around the world pray in Arabic even when it is not their home language. A person who memorizes the whole book is honored with the title *hafiz*.

words.d: the holy book of Islam; the word means "recitation"
a person who has memorized the whole Qur'an
a successor who led the Muslim community after Muhammad

look.title: A Class of Young Reciters
look.text: On a Saturday morning at a mosque in the Chicago suburbs, a group of children sits on the carpet. A teacher recites a short surah in Arabic. The children repeat it line by line. Some of them speak English at home, some Urdu, some Arabic. All of them learn the same words.
look.prompt: Why might a community teach children to recite the Qur'an in Arabic, even if they speak another language at home?

check.q: What does the word Qur'an mean?
check.why: Qur'an means "recitation," because Muslims first learned it by reciting aloud.

check.q: How do most Muslims view an English translation of the Qur'an?
choices: As an explanation of the meaning, not the Qur'an itself
check.why: Muslims believe the Qur'an is fully itself only in Arabic; translations explain its meaning.

check.q: What is a hafiz?
choices: A person who has memorized the whole Qur'an
A tax paid to the poor
check.why: A hafiz has memorized the entire Qur'an.

lessons.title: Surahs, Ayahs and the Sunnah
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an has 114 surahs made of ayahs, and Muslims also learn from the Sunnah, the example of Muhammad recorded in hadith.
reading: The Qur'an is divided into 114 chapters called *surahs*. Each surah is made of verses called *ayahs*. After the short opening surah, the surahs are arranged roughly from longest to shortest. So the Qur'an does not tell one story from start to end, the way a history book might.

The first surah, al-Fatiha ("The Opening"), is only seven verses long. Muslims recite it in every unit of daily prayer. It praises God as merciful and asks to be guided on the straight path. Short surahs near the end, such as Surah 112, are often the first ones children learn.

Muslims also learn from the *Sunnah*, the example of how Muhammad lived. Reports of his words and actions are called *hadith*. Scholars sorted hadith by how reliable their chains of reporters seemed. Sunni and Shia Muslims use partly different hadith collections.

words.d: a chapter of the Qur'an; there are 114
a verse of the Qur'an; the word also means "sign"
the example of Muhammad's life, which Muslims try to follow
a report of something Muhammad said or did

look.title: A Short Surah on One God
look.text: Say: He is God, the One. God, the Eternal, on whom all depend. He does not give birth, and He was not born. And there is none like Him.
look.cite: Qur'an, Surah 112 (al-Ikhlas), verses 1–4; paraphrased in plain English
look.prompt: This surah has only four verses. What does it say God is like, and what does it say God is not like?

check.q: How many surahs are in the Qur'an?
check.why: The Qur'an has 114 surahs.

check.q: How are most surahs of the Qur'an arranged?
choices: In the order of Muhammad's life
check.why: After al-Fatiha, surahs run roughly from longest to shortest.

check.q: What is a hadith?
choices: A report of Muhammad's words or actions
check.why: Hadith are reports of what Muhammad said or did; together they show the Sunnah.

lessons.title: Faith and Prayer
lessons.mainIdea: The first two pillars are the shahada, the statement of faith, and salat, prayer five times a day.
reading: Muslims describe five core practices as the *Five Pillars* of Islam. Like pillars holding up a building, they support a Muslim's life. They appear in a well-known hadith. Sunni and Shia Muslims both keep these practices, though Shia teachers list their core duties a little differently.

The first pillar is the *shahada*, the statement of faith: "There is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God." Saying it sincerely, Muslims believe, is how a person enters Islam. Muslims repeat it in prayer and whisper it to newborn babies.

The second pillar is *salat*, prayer five times a day: at dawn, midday, afternoon, sunset and night. Before praying, Muslims wash in a set way. They face the Kaaba in Mecca, a direction called the qibla. Prayer includes standing, bowing and touching the forehead to the ground.

words.d: five core practices of Islam: shahada, salat, zakat, sawm and hajj
the Muslim statement of faith in one God and in Muhammad as God's messenger
the prayer Muslims perform five times a day
the direction of the Kaaba in Mecca, which Muslims face in prayer

look.title: A Prayer Rug at Lunchtime
look.text: A nurse in a Chicago hospital has a short break at midday. She checks an app that shows the qibla, which from Chicago points roughly northeast. She washes her face, hands and feet, lays down a small rug in a quiet room, and prays for about five minutes before going back to work.
look.prompt: Which parts of salat can you find in this scene? What might a workplace do to make this easier?

check.q: How many times a day do Muslims perform salat?
check.why: Salat is performed five times a day, from dawn to night.

check.q: What is the qibla?
choices: The direction of the Kaaba that Muslims face in prayer
check.why: The qibla is the direction toward the Kaaba in Mecca.

check.q: Which pillar is the statement "There is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God"?
check.why: The shahada is the Muslim statement of faith.

lessons.title: Giving and Fasting
lessons.mainIdea: Zakat is giving part of one's wealth to people in need, and sawm is fasting from dawn to sunset in the month of Ramadan.
reading: The third pillar is *zakat*, giving to those in need. Muslims who have savings above a set amount give a share each year, commonly 2.5 percent. The Qur'an lists who should receive it, including the poor. Muslims believe zakat purifies wealth and reminds them that it comes from God. Many also give extra charity, called sadaqa.

The fourth pillar is *sawm*, fasting during *Ramadan*, the ninth month of the Islamic year. From dawn until sunset, adult Muslims who are able do not eat or drink. Children, the sick, travelers and some others are excused. Many families wake before dawn for a meal and break the fast at sunset.

Muslims believe the Qur'an was first revealed in Ramadan. So many try to read or hear the whole Qur'an during the month, often at special night prayers. The month ends with Eid al-Fitr, the Festival of Breaking the Fast, with prayers, new clothes, gifts and meals.

words.d: required yearly giving of part of one's wealth to people in need
fasting; in Islam, not eating or drinking from dawn to sunset in Ramadan
the ninth month of the Islamic calendar, the month of fasting
the festival that ends Ramadan

look.title: Why Fast?
look.text: You who believe, fasting is prescribed for you, as it was prescribed for those before you, so that you may become mindful of God.
look.cite: Qur'an, Surah 2 (al-Baqarah), verse 183; paraphrased in plain English
look.prompt: According to this verse, what is the purpose of fasting? Who else does the verse say was asked to fast?

check.q: What share of savings do Muslims commonly give each year as zakat?
check.why: Zakat is commonly figured as 2.5 percent of savings above a set amount.

check.q: Which Muslims are excused from the Ramadan fast?
choices: Children, the sick and travelers, among others
People who pray five times a day
check.why: Children, the sick, travelers and some others are excused from sawm.

check.q: Which festival marks the end of Ramadan?
check.why: Eid al-Fitr, the Festival of Breaking the Fast, ends Ramadan.

lessons.title: The Pilgrimage to Mecca
lessons.mainIdea: The hajj is a pilgrimage to Mecca that Muslims who are able should make once in a lifetime.
reading: The fifth pillar is the *hajj*, the pilgrimage to Mecca. It takes place each year in Dhul Hijjah, the last month of the Islamic calendar. Every adult Muslim who is healthy and can afford it is expected to go at least once. In recent years, about two million people have made the hajj at once.

Pilgrims put on simple white clothing called *ihram*. For men it is two unsewn white cloths. Muslims say this shows that everyone is equal before God, rich or poor. Pilgrims walk seven times around the Kaaba and walk between two small hills, remembering Hagar searching for water for her son Ishmael.

Pilgrims also stand in prayer on the plain of Arafat. Then Muslims everywhere celebrate Eid al-Adha, the Festival of the Sacrifice. It remembers the story of Abraham's willingness to sacrifice his son, which appears in the Qur'an. Families share meat with relatives and with the poor.

words.d: the pilgrimage to Mecca that Muslims who are able make once in a lifetime
the simple white clothing and holy state of a pilgrim on hajj
the Festival of the Sacrifice, held during the hajj season

look.title: Two Million in White
look.text: A letter home from the hajj, 1964: an American pilgrim writes that he saw people of every color eating from the same plate and praying side by side. That pilgrim was Malcolm X. He said the experience changed how he thought about race.
look.prompt: Why might the plain white clothing of ihram make pilgrims feel equal? How did the hajj affect Malcolm X, according to his letter?

check.q: Why do pilgrims on hajj wear simple white clothing?
choices: To show that all are equal before God
Because white is the color of Ramadan
To show which tribe they belong to
Because it is the uniform of the caliph
check.why: Muslims say ihram shows equality before God, since rich and poor dress alike.

check.q: Whom do pilgrims remember when they walk between two small hills?
choices: Hagar, searching for water for Ishmael
check.why: Walking between the hills recalls Hagar's search for water for her son Ishmael.

check.q: Which statement about the hajj is correct?
choices: Every Muslim must go every year
It is made in the month of Ramadan
Muslims who are able should go at least once
check.why: The hajj is required once in a lifetime for Muslims who are healthy and can afford it.

lessons.title: Sunni and Shia
lessons.mainIdea: Sunni and Shia Muslims share the Qur'an and the Five Pillars but disagree about who should have led after Muhammad.
reading: After Muhammad died in 632, most of his companions chose Abu Bakr, his close friend, as the first *caliph*. Those who accepted this line of leaders became known as *Sunni* Muslims, from sunnah, "the way." Today most Muslims, about 85 to 90 percent, are Sunni.

Another group believed Muhammad had chosen his cousin and son-in-law, Ali, to lead. They became the *Shia*, from shiat Ali, "the party of Ali." Shia Muslims honor a line of leaders called imams, starting with Ali. Most Shia live in Iran, Iraq, Bahrain, Azerbaijan and Lebanon, with many elsewhere.

In 680, Ali's son Husayn was killed with his small band at Karbala, in Iraq. Shia Muslims mourn him each year on Ashura, the tenth day of the month of Muharram. Sunni and Shia Muslims pray, fast and make the hajj. Many Muslims stress what the two groups share.

words.d: the larger branch of Islam, which accepted the first caliphs chosen by Muhammad's companions
the branch of Islam that holds Ali and his descendants should have led after Muhammad
a prayer leader; for Shia Muslims, also one of the chosen leaders descended from Ali
the tenth of Muharram; Shia Muslims mourn Husayn's death at Karbala on this day

look.title: Two Branches of Islam
look.cite: Common estimates of the world's Muslims; figures vary by source
look.prompt: Sunni estimates run from about 85 to 90 percent. Why might different counts give different numbers?

check.q: What was the first disagreement between Sunni and Shia Muslims about?
choices: Who should lead the community after Muhammad
How many surahs are in the Qur'an
check.why: The split began over leadership after Muhammad's death.

check.q: Whom do Shia Muslims believe should have been the first leader after Muhammad?
check.why: Shia means "party of Ali"; they hold that Ali should have led.

check.q: What do Shia Muslims remember on Ashura?
choices: The death of Husayn at Karbala in 680
check.why: On Ashura, Shia Muslims mourn Husayn, killed at Karbala in 680.

lessons.title: The Mosque and the Moon
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims gather at the mosque, especially for Friday prayer, and follow a lunar calendar whose months move through the seasons.
reading: A *mosque* is a place where Muslims pray together. The Arabic word masjid means "place of bowing down." Inside there are no statues or pictures of people. A niche in the wall, the mihrab, shows the qibla. Many mosques have a tall tower called a minaret, from which the call to prayer is given.

At midday on Friday, Muslims gather for jumu'ah, the congregational prayer. A leader gives a short sermon, then leads the prayer. Men are expected to attend. Women may attend and often pray in their own section. Mosques also hold classes, weddings, meals and community events.

The *Islamic calendar* follows the moon. Each month begins with the new crescent moon, so the year has about 354 days. That is about 11 days shorter than the solar year. So Ramadan comes about 11 days earlier each year and moves through every season over about 33 years.

words.d: a Muslim place of prayer; in Arabic, masjid
a tall tower of a mosque, from which the call to prayer is given
the Friday midday prayer that Muslims pray together
a calendar of 12 moon-based months that counts years from the hijra

look.title: Moon Year and Sun Year
rows: Days Ramadan moves earlier each year
Years for Ramadan to circle all seasons
look.cite: Standard calendar facts; the lunar year has 354 or 355 days
look.prompt: If Ramadan begins in March one year, about when will it begin three years later?

check.q: When do Muslims gather for their weekly congregational prayer?
check.why: Jumu'ah is the Friday midday prayer.

check.q: Why does Ramadan come at a different time each year on the everyday calendar?
choices: The Islamic calendar follows the moon and is about 11 days shorter
Each mosque picks its own date

check.why: The mihrab is a niche that marks the qibla, the direction of the Kaaba.

review.q: Why did people in Mecca call Muhammad al-Amin?
choices: He was the chief of the Quraysh
review.why: Al-Amin means "the trustworthy," his reputation before he began to preach.

review.q: Put these events in order: hijra, first revelation, return to Mecca.
choices: Hijra, first revelation, return to Mecca
Return to Mecca, hijra, first revelation
First revelation, return to Mecca, hijra
First revelation, hijra, return to Mecca
review.why: The first revelation (c. 610) came before the hijra (622) and the return to Mecca (630).

choices: Surah: a chapter of the Qur'an
review.why: A surah is a chapter of the Qur'an; the other pairs mix up terms.

choices: The same view of who should lead after Muhammad
The same hadith collections in every case
The Qur'an and the Five Pillars
The mourning of Ashura as their main holiday

review.q: A student says, "Muslims fast all day and night for a month." What correction fits?
choices: They fast from dawn to sunset during Ramadan
They fast only during the hajj
They fast for one day on Eid

choices: Arabic is the only language Muslims speak
Muslims believe the Qur'an is God's word in Arabic

review.why: Eid al-Adha, the Festival of the Sacrifice, recalls Abraham's story.

chapters.title: Caliphates, Learning and the Wider World
chapters.bigQuestion: How did Muslim states, scholars and traders connect so much of the world, and how did Islam come to America?

story.title: Gold and Books Across the Sahara
story.kicker: A caravan crosses the desert toward Timbuktu, carrying salt, gold, cloth and books.
paragraphs: The Sahara, around the year 1350. A long line of camels moves across the sand in the cool hours before sunrise. Some carry slabs of salt cut from desert mines. Others carry cloth, copper and paper. The guides watch the stars and the shapes of the dunes to find their way.

The traders are heading south, toward the Niger River and the empire of Mali. Mali is rich in gold. North African merchants trade salt for it, since salt is scarce in the lands farther south. Along with goods, the traders bring something else: books written in Arabic.

At the end of the road lies Timbuktu. The city has mosques built of sun-dried mud brick, with wooden beams sticking out of the walls. Students gather around teachers to study the Qur'an, law, grammar, astronomy and medicine. Families copy books by hand and keep them in wooden chests.

A generation earlier, Mali's ruler, Mansa Musa, had made the hajj to Mecca. Writers of the time said he carried so much gold that its price fell in Cairo when he passed through. He came home with scholars and builders. Timbuktu grew into a center of learning.

The same faith that began in Mecca had now reached West Africa, Spain, Persia and India. This chapter follows how that happened: through rulers and armies, but also through traders, teachers, translators and ordinary families.
story.think: The caravan carried salt, gold and books. Which of those do you think changed Timbuktu the most over time? Why?

lessons.title: The First Four Caliphs
lessons.mainIdea: After Muhammad, four caliphs led the Muslim community from 632 to 661, and Muslim rule spread quickly beyond Arabia.
reading: A *caliphate* is a state led by a caliph, a successor to Muhammad as leader of the community. The first four caliphs were Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali. They ruled from 632 to 661. Sunni Muslims call them the *Rashidun*, or "rightly guided" caliphs. Shia Muslims honor Ali as the first rightful imam.

In these years, Arab Muslim armies defeated much of the Byzantine and Persian empires. They took Syria, Iraq, Egypt and Persia. Historians note that most people in these lands did not become Muslim right away. Conversion happened slowly, over centuries.

Jews and Christians under Muslim rule were often treated as *dhimmi*, protected peoples. They could keep their faith and their places of worship. They paid a special tax, the jizya, and faced some limits. How they were treated changed from ruler to ruler and from place to place.

words.d: a state ruled by a caliph, a successor to Muhammad's leadership
"rightly guided"; the Sunni name for the first four caliphs
a protected non-Muslim, usually a Jew or Christian, living under Muslim rule

look.title: Fast Conquest, Slow Conversion
look.text: Within about 30 years of Muhammad's death, Muslim rulers governed lands from Egypt to Persia. Yet historians estimate that in many of these lands, Muslims did not become the majority for two or three centuries or more.
look.prompt: Why might ruling a land and changing people's religion happen at very different speeds?

check.q: Who were the four Rashidun caliphs, in order?
choices: Mansa Musa, Abu Bakr, Ali, Umar
check.why: The first four caliphs were Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali.

check.q: What did the jizya tax mean for Jews and Christians under early Muslim rule?
choices: They had to leave the country
They were forced to become Muslim
They paid a tax and could keep their faith
check.why: As dhimmi, they paid the jizya and kept their religion, with some limits.

check.q: How fast did most people in newly ruled lands become Muslim?
check.why: Historians describe conversion as slow, often taking centuries.

lessons.title: The Umayyads of Damascus
lessons.mainIdea: The Umayyad caliphs ruled from Damascus from 661 to 750, over an empire stretching from Spain to Central Asia.
reading: In 661 a governor named Muawiya founded the *Umayyad* caliphate. He made Damascus, in Syria, his capital. Leadership now passed from father to son, like a royal family. The Umayyads ruled until 750.

Under the Umayyads, Muslim rule reached across North Africa and into Spain in 711. In the east it reached Central Asia and the Indus River. Arabic became the language of government. The Umayyads made the first Islamic coins with only words on them, no pictures.

The Umayyads built famous buildings. The Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem was completed around 691. The Great Mosque of Damascus followed soon after. Both used mosaics of plants and patterns instead of pictures of people. Some Muslims criticized the Umayyads for living like kings, and in 750 a rival family overthrew them.

words.d: the family of caliphs who ruled from Damascus from 661 to 750
a picture or pattern made from many small pieces of colored stone or glass

look.title: A Coin Without a Face
look.text: Before about 696, coins used in Muslim lands often copied Byzantine or Persian coins, with rulers' faces. Then the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik issued gold coins with only Arabic writing, including words about one God.
look.prompt: What message might a coin with only writing send to people who used it every day?

check.q: Which city was the Umayyad capital?
check.why: The Umayyads ruled from Damascus in Syria.

check.q: Which building was completed in Jerusalem under the Umayyads around 691?
check.why: The Dome of the Rock was completed around 691 under Umayyad rule.

check.q: How did leadership change under the Umayyads?
choices: It passed from father to son within one family
It was chosen by a vote of all Muslims
It was chosen by the Byzantine emperor
It was given to Ali's descendants
check.why: The Umayyads made the caliphate pass within their family.

lessons.title: The Abbasids of Baghdad
lessons.mainIdea: The Abbasids ruled from 750 and built Baghdad, a round city that became one of the largest in the world.
reading: In 750 the *Abbasid* family overthrew the Umayyads. They moved the capital east to Iraq. In 762 the caliph al-Mansur founded Baghdad on the Tigris River. It was planned as a round city with the palace and great mosque in the middle.

Baghdad sat on trade routes between the Mediterranean, Persia, India and China. Ships and caravans brought silk, spices, paper and ideas. Historians estimate that by about 900 it was one of the largest cities in the world, with many hundreds of thousands of people.

Over time, Abbasid power weakened. Local rulers took control of many regions, though they often still named the caliph in Friday prayers. In 1258 the Mongols captured and destroyed much of Baghdad and killed the caliph. Historians often mark that year as the end of an age.

words.d: the family of caliphs who ruled from Baghdad from 750 to 1258
a people from Central Asia whose armies built a huge empire in the 1200s

look.title: The Early Caliphates
look.cite: Standard dates used by historians of the Islamic world
look.prompt: Which caliphate lasted longest? About how many years did it last?

check.q: Who founded the city of Baghdad in 762?
check.why: The Abbasid caliph al-Mansur founded Baghdad in 762.

check.q: Why did Baghdad grow so rich?
choices: It was in the middle of the Sahara
It sat on trade routes linking many regions
It was the site of the Kaaba
check.why: Baghdad lay on routes linking the Mediterranean, Persia, India and China.

check.q: What happened to Baghdad in 1258?
choices: It became the capital of Spain
The Mongols captured it and killed the caliph
check.why: In 1258 the Mongols sacked Baghdad and ended Abbasid rule there.

lessons.title: The House of Wisdom
lessons.mainIdea: In Abbasid Baghdad, scholars of many faiths translated Greek, Persian and Indian books into Arabic and added new ideas.
reading: Under the Abbasids, especially in the 800s, Baghdad became a center of *translation*. Scholars turned books on philosophy, medicine, math and astronomy from Greek, Persian, Syriac and Sanskrit into Arabic. A library and study center often called the *House of Wisdom* is linked to this work. Historians still debate exactly how large and formal it was.

The translators came from many backgrounds. Some were Muslims. Many were Christians, such as Hunayn ibn Ishaq, who translated Greek medical books. Others were Jews or followers of other faiths. They shared Arabic as a common language of learning.

Muslim scholars did not only copy old books. They checked, argued with and added to them. Many Muslims pointed to the Qur'an and hadith that praise knowledge. Centuries later, many of these Arabic books were translated into Latin in Spain and Italy and helped shape learning in Europe.

words.d: turning writing from one language into another
a library and study center in Abbasid Baghdad linked to translation and science

look.title: A Prayer for Knowledge
look.text: Say: My Lord, increase me in knowledge.
look.cite: Qur'an, Surah 20 (Ta Ha), verse 114; paraphrased in plain English
look.prompt: How might a verse like this encourage scholars in Baghdad? Can you think of a text from another tradition that praises learning?

check.q: What was the main work linked to the House of Wisdom?
choices: Translating and studying books from many languages
check.why: Scholars in Baghdad translated Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic and studied them.

check.q: Who was Hunayn ibn Ishaq?
choices: A Christian scholar who translated Greek medical books
check.why: Hunayn ibn Ishaq was a Christian translator of Greek medicine into Arabic.

check.q: How did Arabic learning later reach Europe?
choices: Through Latin translations made in Spain and Italy
check.why: Many Arabic works were translated into Latin in Spain and Italy.

lessons.title: Algebra and the Stars
lessons.mainIdea: Scholars in the Muslim world advanced math and astronomy; the word algebra comes from al-Khwarizmi's book.
reading: Around 820, a scholar in Baghdad named Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi wrote a book on solving equations. Its title included the Arabic word al-jabr, meaning "restoring." That word became our word *algebra*. The word algorithm comes from a Latin form of his name.

Scholars in the Muslim world also used the numerals that came from India, including zero. Arabic writers spread them west. Europeans learned them later and called them "Arabic numerals." These are the digits 0 to 9 you use today.

*Astronomy*, the study of the stars and planets, had practical uses for Muslims. They needed to find the qibla from any place, set prayer times by the sun and spot the new moon to begin each month. Astronomers built observatories and improved the astrolabe, a tool for measuring the height of stars.

words.d: math that uses letters or symbols for unknown numbers; the name comes from Arabic al-jabr
the study of the stars, planets and sky
a tool for measuring the height of the sun or stars, used to tell time and direction

look.title: Why Write a Math Book?
look.text: Al-Khwarizmi explains that he wrote a short book on calculating, to help with things people need every day: dividing inheritances, making wills, trade and business, lawsuits, measuring land and digging canals.
look.cite: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, preface to The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing (c. 820); summarized
look.prompt: What everyday problems did al-Khwarizmi want his math to solve? Which one surprises you?

check.q: Where does the word algebra come from?
choices: The Arabic word al-jabr in al-Khwarizmi's book
check.why: Algebra comes from al-jabr in the title of al-Khwarizmi's book.

check.q: Why did astronomy matter for Muslim religious practice?
choices: It helped find the qibla, set prayer times and mark new months
It was needed to choose the caliph
It decided who could go on hajj
It set the amount of zakat
check.why: The qibla, prayer times and lunar months all depend on the sky.

check.q: Where did the numerals 0 to 9 first come from, before Arabic writers spread them?
check.why: The numerals came from India; Arabic writers carried them west.

lessons.title: Medicine and Paper
lessons.mainIdea: Muslim-ruled cities built hospitals, produced great medical books and spread paper-making from China to the West.
reading: Many cities in the Muslim world had hospitals, called *bimaristan* in Persian. Some cared for patients of any faith, for free, and trained doctors. The Persian scholar Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, wrote The Canon of Medicine around 1025. European medical schools used a Latin translation of it for centuries.

*Paper* came from China. Paper-making reached Samarkand in Central Asia by the 700s. By the late 700s, Baghdad had paper mills. Paper was much cheaper than parchment made from animal skin. So books became easier to make, and libraries and bookshops spread.

Paper-making moved west through Egypt and North Africa to Spain. From there it reached the rest of Europe. Centuries later, cheap paper helped make the printing press useful. The same roads that carried scholars also carried their tools.

words.d: a hospital in the medieval Muslim world
a writing material made from plant fibers, invented in China and spread west through Muslim lands
a writing material made from animal skin

look.title: One Book, Two Prices
look.text: Imagine two copies of the same book around 900. One is written on parchment, which takes the skins of many animals. The other is written on paper made from old rags and plant fibers in a Baghdad mill.
look.prompt: Which copy would cost less? What would change in a city if books became much cheaper?

check.q: Who wrote The Canon of Medicine?
check.why: Ibn Sina wrote The Canon of Medicine around 1025.

check.q: Where was paper first invented?
check.why: Paper came from China and spread west through Muslim lands.

check.q: Why did paper help learning spread?
choices: It was cheaper than parchment, so books cost less
It replaced the need to read
check.why: Paper made books cheaper, so more libraries and bookshops opened.

lessons.title: Al-Andalus and Córdoba
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims ruled much of Spain, called al-Andalus, for centuries, and Córdoba became a great city of learning.
reading: In 711, Muslim forces from North Africa crossed into Spain. Muslims called the lands they ruled *al-Andalus*. When the Abbasids overthrew the Umayyads, one Umayyad prince escaped to Spain. In 756 he set up his own state with Córdoba as its capital. In 929 his descendant declared himself caliph.

Córdoba grew into one of Europe's largest cities. Work on its Great Mosque began in 785, with rows of red-and-white striped arches. The city had libraries, markets and paved streets. Muslims, Jews and Christians all lived there. The Jewish thinker Maimonides and the Muslim thinker Ibn Rushd were both born in Córdoba in the 1100s.

People sometimes call this time *convivencia*, "living together." Historians say that is partly true. There was real sharing of ideas and art, and also times of conflict and harsh rule. Christian kingdoms slowly took back the land. Granada, the last Muslim kingdom, fell in 1492.

words.d: the Arabic name for the parts of Spain and Portugal under Muslim rule
Spanish for "living together"; a name for times when Muslims, Jews and Christians shared life in Spain

look.title: One Building, Two Faiths
look.text: In 1236 Christian forces took Córdoba. They turned the Great Mosque into a cathedral. In the 1500s a church was built in the middle of it. Today visitors walk through the striped arches of the mosque and then into the cathedral inside.
look.prompt: What can one building tell you about a city's history? What questions might a visitor ask?

check.q: What was al-Andalus?
choices: The Muslim-ruled parts of Spain and Portugal
check.why: Al-Andalus was the Arabic name for Muslim-ruled Iberia.

check.q: Which two thinkers were born in Córdoba in the 1100s?
check.why: Maimonides (Jewish) and Ibn Rushd (Muslim) were both born in Córdoba.

check.q: What happened in 1492 in Spain?
choices: Granada, the last Muslim kingdom, fell
check.why: Granada fell to the Christian kingdoms in 1492.

lessons.title: Mali, Mansa Musa and Timbuktu
lessons.mainIdea: Islam spread to West Africa along trade routes, and Mali's ruler Mansa Musa made Timbuktu a center of learning.
reading: Islam reached West Africa mostly through trade, not conquest. Muslim merchants crossed the Sahara with salt and goods, trading for gold. Some West African rulers and traders became Muslim. Many ordinary people kept older local practices for a long time, and some blended them with Islam.

The empire of *Mali* became rich from gold. Its most famous ruler, Mansa Musa, made the hajj in 1324. Writers of the time reported that he brought huge amounts of gold, which lowered its price in Cairo. He returned with scholars and an architect who worked on mosques in Timbuktu and Gao.

*Timbuktu* became known for its scholars and books. Students studied at mosques such as Sankore. Families there have kept hundreds of thousands of handwritten manuscripts, on law, astronomy, medicine and poetry. In 2012 and 2013, people in Timbuktu hid many of them to protect them during a war.

words.d: a West African empire, rich in gold, at its height in the 1300s
a city in Mali famous for its mosques, scholars and manuscripts
a book or document written by hand

look.title: A Traveler in Mali
look.text: The traveler Ibn Battuta writes that the people of Mali are careful about their prayers, that crowds fill the mosque on Friday, and that parents make their children memorize the Qur'an. He also praises the safety of the roads, where travelers need not fear robbers.
look.cite: Ibn Battuta, the Rihla (Travels), account of his visit to Mali in 1352–1353; summarized
look.prompt: What does Ibn Battuta notice about religion in Mali? Why might a traveler care about the safety of the roads?

check.q: How did Islam mostly reach West Africa?
check.why: Merchants crossing the Sahara brought Islam to West Africa.

check.q: What is Mansa Musa best known for?
choices: His rich hajj in 1324 and building up Timbuktu
check.why: Mansa Musa's 1324 hajj was famous for its gold, and he brought scholars home.

check.q: What is Timbuktu famous for today?
check.why: Timbuktu is known for its mosques, scholars and many manuscripts.

lessons.title: The Ottoman Empire
lessons.mainIdea: The Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453 and ruled a large Muslim empire until after World War I.
reading: The *Ottomans* began as a small Turkish state in Anatolia around 1300. In 1453 Sultan Mehmed II captured Constantinople, the Byzantine capital. The city became the Ottoman capital, later known as Istanbul. The great church Hagia Sophia was turned into a mosque.

At its height in the 1500s, under Suleiman the Magnificent, the empire ruled Southeast Europe, Turkey, the Middle East and North Africa. It also governed Mecca and Medina. Ottoman sultans used the title caliph. The architect Sinan designed many famous mosques, with large domes and slim minarets.

The Ottomans organized many non-Muslim communities into groups often called *millets*. Greek Orthodox Christians, Armenian Christians and Jews each ran many of their own religious and family matters. The empire ended after World War I. Turkey abolished the office of caliph in 1924.

words.d: a Turkish Muslim dynasty that ruled a large empire from about 1300 to 1922
a title for a Muslim ruler
in the Ottoman Empire, a religious community that ran many of its own affairs

look.title: A Dome in Istanbul
look.text: Hagia Sophia was built as a church in 537. It became a mosque in 1453, with minarets added outside. In 1934 Turkey made it a museum. In 2020 it became a mosque again, and visitors of any faith may still enter outside prayer times.
look.prompt: Why might one building mean different things to Christians, Muslims and historians?

check.q: What happened in 1453?
check.why: Mehmed II took Constantinople in 1453; it became Istanbul.

check.q: What was a millet in the Ottoman Empire?
choices: A religious community that ran many of its own affairs
check.why: Millets let groups such as Orthodox Christians and Jews manage many of their own matters.

check.q: Who designed many famous Ottoman mosques?
check.why: Sinan was the leading Ottoman architect of the 1500s.

lessons.title: Islam in South and Southeast Asia
lessons.mainIdea: Today most Muslims live in Asia, and Indonesia has more Muslims than any other country.
reading: Many people picture Islam mainly in the Middle East. In fact, most Muslims today live in South and Southeast Asia. Islam reached India through conquest, trade and teachers. The *Mughal* emperors ruled much of India from 1526. Their buildings include the Taj Mahal, a tomb completed around 1653.

In India, *Sufis*, Muslims who seek to feel close to God through prayer and devotion, drew many followers. Their shrines became places of pilgrimage for people of several faiths. Today India, Pakistan and Bangladesh together are home to hundreds of millions of Muslims.

Islam reached the islands of Southeast Asia mainly through merchants and Sufi teachers, starting around the 1200s. Today *Indonesia* has more Muslims than any other country. Its Muslims mix Islam with local languages, arts and customs. Malaysia and Brunei also have Muslim majorities.

words.d: a Muslim dynasty that ruled much of India from 1526
a Muslim who follows a path of seeking closeness to God through prayer, poetry and devotion
a country of many islands in Southeast Asia; it has the most Muslims of any country

look.title: Countries With the Most Muslims
look.cite: Rounded common estimates for the 2020s; figures vary by source
look.prompt: How many of these six countries are in Asia? What does this show about where Muslims live?

check.q: Which country has the most Muslims?
check.why: Indonesia has the largest Muslim population of any country.

check.q: How did Islam mainly reach Southeast Asia?
check.why: Traders and Sufi teachers carried Islam to the islands of Southeast Asia.

check.q: What is a Sufi?
choices: A Muslim who seeks closeness to God through devotion
check.why: Sufis follow a devotional path of seeking closeness to God.

lessons.title: Muslims in America
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims have been in America since the time of slavery, and today Chicago has one of the country's largest Muslim communities.
reading: The first large group of Muslims in America came in chains. Historians estimate that a meaningful share of the enslaved West Africans brought to the Americas were Muslim. One of them, *Omar ibn Said*, was enslaved in North Carolina. In 1831 he wrote a short life story in Arabic.

Later, Muslims came as immigrants from the Middle East, South Asia and Africa. In the 1900s, some Black Americans formed new movements. The Nation of Islam, founded in Detroit in 1930, later made Chicago its headquarters. Its teachings differed from mainstream Islam. In 1975 Warith Deen Mohammed led many members toward Sunni Islam.

Today Chicago and its suburbs are home to many mosques. They serve Muslims with roots in Palestine, Pakistan, India, Bosnia, Somalia, Nigeria and many other places, as well as Black American and convert Muslims. Many mosques run schools, food pantries and free clinics. Muslims in America are one of the country's most diverse faith groups.

words.d: an enslaved West African Muslim scholar who wrote his life story in Arabic in 1831
a person who moves to a new country to live
a movement founded in Detroit in 1930, later based in Chicago, whose teachings differ from mainstream Islam

look.title: A Life Story in Arabic
look.text: Omar ibn Said writes that he was born in Futa Toro in West Africa and studied for many years with teachers there. He tells how he was captured, carried across the sea and sold, and how he came to live in North Carolina. He opens with a surah from the Qur'an.
look.cite: Omar ibn Said, The Life of Omar ibn Said (1831), written in Arabic; summarized
look.prompt: Why is it important that Omar ibn Said wrote his own story? What does his Arabic writing show about his life before slavery?

check.q: Who was Omar ibn Said?
choices: The founder of the Nation of Islam
An enslaved West African Muslim who wrote his life story in Arabic
check.why: Omar ibn Said, enslaved in North Carolina, wrote his story in Arabic in 1831.

check.q: What did Warith Deen Mohammed do in 1975?
choices: He led many Nation of Islam members toward Sunni Islam
He made the first hajj from America
He wrote The Canon of Medicine
check.why: Warith Deen Mohammed guided many members toward mainstream Sunni Islam.

check.q: Which statement best describes Muslims in America today?
choices: They all come from one country
They are all members of the Nation of Islam
They are a very diverse group with roots in many places
check.why: American Muslims include immigrants from many lands, Black American Muslims and converts.

review.q: Put these capitals in the order they became caliphate capitals: Baghdad, Medina, Damascus.
review.why: The first caliphs led from Medina, the Umayyads from Damascus, then the Abbasids from Baghdad.

review.q: Which scholar gave his name to the word algorithm?
review.why: Algorithm comes from a Latin form of al-Khwarizmi's name.

review.q: What did Muslims, Jews and Christians share in al-Andalus at its best?
choices: One single ruler for all time
Cities, ideas and learning, alongside times of conflict
review.why: Al-Andalus saw real sharing of ideas and also conflict, as historians describe it.

review.q: Which traveler wrote about the mosques and safe roads of Mali?
review.why: Ibn Battuta visited Mali in 1352–1353 and described it in the Rihla.

review.q: Why was paper so important to learning in the Muslim world?
choices: It was cheaper than parchment, so books spread
Only the Qur'an could be written on it
review.why: Paper, from China, made books cheaper and helped libraries grow.

review.q: What happened to Hagia Sophia in 1453?
choices: It was built as a church
It was turned into a mosque
review.why: After the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453, Hagia Sophia became a mosque.

review.q: Which region is home to most Muslims today?
review.why: Most Muslims live in Asia; Indonesia, Pakistan, India and Bangladesh have the largest populations.

review.q: How did Islam spread to West Africa and Southeast Asia, compared with Syria and Egypt?
choices: Mostly through trade and teachers, not conquest
Only through conquest in all four
review.why: Syria and Egypt came under Muslim rule by conquest; West Africa and Southeast Asia were reached mostly by merchants and teachers.
